analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for seniors and funds them by phasing out the payroll tax cap on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would phase out the Social Security payroll tax cap and raise benefits, never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to three House committees on July 21, 2022 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how Social Security works in three main ways. It would raise cost-of-living increases for beneficiaries by using a price index that better matches what seniors buy. It would phase out the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes, so high earners would pay Social Security taxes on all their earnings, while earning modestly higher benefits on that income. And it would extend benefits through the month a beneficiary dies, so a final prorated check goes to the estate rather than disappearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries would gain in several ways: annual cost-of-living increases would be calculated using a price index that tracks what people 62 and older actually buy, which typically rises faster than the index now used [S3]. Benefits would continue through the month a beneficiary dies, with the final month paid on a prorated basis to the estate or a named payee [S3]. A fix would prevent an unintended drop in benefits tied to the wage-index formula [S3]. Higher earners would also earn credit toward slightly higher benefits on their earnings above the cap [S3]. Over the long run, taxpayers and beneficiaries both gain from a program whose financing is put on firmer footing.

how_it_helps.text: Cost-of-living increases would be tied to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, an index built around the spending of people 62 and older, which generally shows faster inflation for seniors than the index now used.
Benefits would continue through the month a beneficiary dies, and the final month would be paid prorated by days, to the estate or a named payee, instead of being lost entirely.

The bill would eliminate, over seven years, the cap on wages and self-employment income subject to Social Security taxes, applying the tax to a shrinking share (86% in 2023, down to zero percent excluded after 2028) of earnings above the cap — a step that would improve the program's financing without cutting anyone's benefits.
Higher earners would not pay the new taxes for nothing: a new 'surplus earnings' benefit formula would give them credit toward higher benefits on income above the cap.
A technical fix would prevent an unintended drop in benefits caused by how the national average wage index is applied.

analysis.who_pays: High earners — workers and self-employed people making above the annual wage cap (about $147,000 in 2022) — would pay Social Security payroll taxes on wages above the cap, phased in fully by 2029; their employers would pay the matching share on those wages too [S3]. Higher earners would receive somewhat larger benefits in return, which offsets part of the added revenue [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: Phasing out the payroll tax cap would raise taxes on high earners and add a payroll tax cost for their employers — a large, immediate tax increase on households and businesses above the wage cap, even though the same earners would get some offsetting benefit credit.

Giving higher earners credit toward larger benefits on income above the cap (3% of surplus earnings up to a threshold, then 0.25%) would return part of the new revenue, reducing how much the tax change strengthens the program's finances.
Extending benefits through the month of death and paying a prorated final check to estates would add new program costs on top of the benefit increases.

Critics of lifting the cap argue it changes Social Security's traditional link between what a worker pays in and what they receive, since benefits would no longer track contributions at the top of the earnings scale — a fairness concern even though the bill softens it with the surplus-earnings credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for beneficiaries are concrete and broadly shared: a more accurate inflation index for seniors, an extra month of benefits for surviving families, and a benefit-calculation fix. The costs fall on a relatively narrow group — high earners and their employers — though giving those earners benefit credit would trim the revenue gain. The main weakness is not design but fate: the bill was never debated, so its financing assumptions and tradeoffs were never examined or tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Ways and Means Committee after referral and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 21, 2022 and referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor Committees, and then to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security.
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the action history for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted only its sponsor and three cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, but the burden of acting on Social Security's finances was lifted from the 117th Congress, and the highest-earning households avoided a phased-in payroll tax increase that never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died untouched

sides.party_line_note: Only four House Democrats were involved as sponsor or cosponsors, and no Republican ever took a recorded position for or against; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows the split.

industries.note: They would pay Social Security payroll tax on wages above the annual cap, phased in between 2023 and 2029; employers pay a matching share. In exchange, high earners would earn modestly larger benefits on that income.
